PART EIGHT
Faith & Doubt
CHAPTER 69
When You Have Doubts
About God
A question you once put aside has become difficult to ignore.
Perhaps it concerns something in Scripture, the credibility of
the resurrection, or whether belief in a good God can survive
what you have seen. Familiar answers may sound different now.
You might also be wondering what would happen if people knew
you were asking.
It helps to give the question its own words before deciding what
it means about your entire faith. “I do not understand this
passage” is a different concern from “I no longer know whether
God exists.” Disappointment with Christians may involve
questions about their conduct as well as what you believe about
Christ. Each deserves to be heard accurately.
You need not present the question more politely than you can
honestly manage. You can bring it into prayer, including
uncertainty about whether anyone is listening. A conversation
with a thoughtful Christian can also begin before you know
what conclusion you will reach.

Thomas is addressed directly
In John 20, Thomas is absent when the risen Jesus first appears
to the gathered disciples. When they tell him they have seen the
Lord, he refuses to believe unless he sees the marks of the nails
and can put his hand into Jesus' side.
Eight days later, the disciples are together again, and Thomas is
with them. Jesus comes among them and invites Thomas to look
at His hands and reach toward His side. He also calls him to stop
doubting and believe. Thomas responds by addressing Jesus as
his Lord and his God.
Jesus addresses the objection Thomas had stated and calls him
toward belief. John does not say whether Thomas actually
touches the wounds before answering.
Jesus then speaks of the blessedness of those who believe
without having seen. Later in the chapter, John explains why he
has written: so that readers may believe that Jesus is the Christ,
the Son of God, and have life in His name. For those of us who
were not in that room, his written testimony gives something to
examine.
Choose a question you can examine
If everything seems uncertain at once, begin with the concern
that is most pressing. What exactly would you like to
understand? What has led you to question it? Is there a claim
you need to investigate, or an experience you need someone to
hear before offering an argument?
For a question about a biblical passage, read what comes before
and after it. Notice who is speaking, to whom, and about what. A
sentence that sounds like a private promise when isolated may
belong to a particular event or a letter to a community.
Understanding the context may clarify the question, even when
it does not resolve every difficulty.

For a historical or philosophical concern, seek a careful
treatment of that actual subject. Ask whether an author explains
objections fairly and distinguishes evidence from
interpretation. Look for the support an argument gives for its
conclusions. A knowledgeable person may be able to help you
compare accounts and recognize what each one claims.
Give yourself room to consider what you find. Constantly
moving from one argument to its reply can leave you with many
impressions and little understanding. After reading, try stating
what the argument claims and what remains unanswered. You
may discover that the next question is smaller and more precise
than the first.
Belief can include asking for help
Mark 9 records a father bringing his suffering son to Jesus after
the disciples have been unable to help. His appeal includes
uncertainty about what Jesus can do. When Jesus speaks to him
about believing, the father answers:
Immediately the boy’s father cried out, “I do believe; help my
unbelief!”
Mark 9:24, Berean Standard Bible
His words hold belief and a need for help in the same prayer.
Jesus goes on to deliver the boy; that outcome is not a test of the
certainty another suffering family must achieve. You can use
the father's words to bring God the faith you have and the
difficulty you are facing.
You may continue some practices while examining your beliefs.
Reading a Gospel, joining a conversation, or asking someone to
pray with you need not mean claiming that every question has
been settled. Be clear about where you are. A person who can
accompany you patiently will not require you to report a
stronger conviction than you have.

If someone you care about has doubts about God
Ask what they are questioning. Listen before deciding that you
already know the argument or the experience behind it. Jude
1:22 calls for mercy toward those who doubt. Let that instruction
shape the conversation, including your response when you
cannot answer.
Offer to look into a question together. Admit the limits of your
knowledge and avoid treating a quick reply as the end of their
inquiry. Keep ordinary friendship available. Affection that
disappears when someone asks a hard question can make it
difficult for them to trust the next conversation.
For reflection
• How would you state your most pressing question in a sentence
that describes it accurately?
• What would help you examine it: context, evidence, or a
conversation about an experience?
• Who could listen without demanding a conclusion before you
are ready to give one?
Prayer
God, these are the questions I have. Help me seek truth honestly and
recognize what I do not yet understand. Give me patient people to
think with, and courage to examine what I find. Where I believe,
help me grow; where I struggle, meet me with mercy. Amen.
For further reading: John 20:24–31; Mark 9:17–29; Jude 1:20–23; Psalm 10:1–2.

When Christians Have Hurt You (p. 349).
